title: Developer Goes Into Debt Spending $1,000 A Day To Keep Steam Demo For AI-Fueled Driving Sim Going
key_facts: Teach My Little Sister How To Drive is an upcoming driving-test (DMV) simulator from the developer Easy Fox; the player coaches a chatbot that plays a chaotic young learner driver.
Easy Fox says in a Steam update that demo players grew more than twentyfold over the past month, which raised its operating costs considerably.

The chatbot first ran on Google's Gemini; heavy demo use caused usage-limit errors and Google told the studio there was no easy way out, so it switched to an OpenAI model while hoping to fix the Gemini problem.

Easy Fox says the surge forced it to take out a bank loan; Kotaku says keeping the demo running apparently costs more than $1,000 a day, which the studio admits it will have to factor into the game's price.
Easy Fox is a team of four and says financial pressure may force it to close the demo before the full release; it says it has not made that decision.
The update also answers complaints that the AI-run sister does not follow instructions as wanted.
Kotaku's own view: the case is an amusing example of AI's unclear profitability (opinion, not reported fact).
quote_evidence: Over the past month, the number of demo players has grown more than twentyfold
However, we are a small team of four, and financial pressure may mean we have to close the demo earlier than expected before the full release.
We have not made that decision at this time.
why_it_matters_hint: Live AI chat costs the developer money for every player, so a free demo can become a debt for a small studio.
event_date: Steam update described as the latest on 10 Oct 2026; its exact date is not stated.
notes: Kotaku's own reporting, quoting the studio's Steam update; the Steam page itself was not opened. The $1,000 a day figure is Kotaku's wording ('apparently'), not a quote from the studio.
